summary: Defines a Management Information Base module for logging SNMP notifications, so a managed device can keep a record of the alerts it sent. Managers can read the log later, even if some notifications were missed. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A diary where a device writes down every alarm it rang, so someone can read the diary later even if they were not around when the alarm sounded.

subtitle: An SNMP MIB that keeps a log of notifications so managers can catch up on alerts they missed.

tldr.problem: SNMP Traps and Informs can be lost, for example when Informs exceed their retransmission limits, so a manager may never learn that something happened.
tldr.mechanism: The Notification Log MIB gives a system a local log of notifications, with configuration objects, statistics counters and log tables that a manager can poll later.
tldr.outcome: Other MIBs need to do less to preserve event details, and applications can poll the log to check that they have not missed important notifications.

today: RFC 3014 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2000, and it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why Log Notifications
sections.content:
Systems that support SNMP often need to record notification information as a hedge against lost notifications. These are Traps or Informs (RFC 1905) that exceed their retransmission limits. This MIB provides a common local logging function for other MIBs to use. It is intended mainly for senders of notifications but could also be used by receivers.

With the log in place, individual MIBs carry less responsibility for recording the transient details of an event in case the message is lost, and applications can poll the log to verify they have not missed important notifications.

The module is written in SMIv2. Section 1 of the RFC also gives the usual overview of the SNMP Management Framework and its components, which this explainer does not repeat.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a shouted warning is not heard. The log is a notebook where the warning is also written down, so you can read it afterwards.

sections.title: Engines, Contexts and Named Logs
sections.content:
A log can collect two flows of notifications: ones received from one or more SNMP engines as informs and traps, and ones delivered to the engine by some other mechanism at the interface to the notification originator. The second flow is modeled as the engine sending a notification to itself.

A system may have several SNMP engines, each with its own engine identification, and an engine may have several named management contexts. To understand a logged notification you need to know which engine and context it came from, so the MIB records the source engine ID and the context name.

The MIB also has named logs. With log names and view-based access control (RFC 2575), an administrator can give different users different access. A system with fewer resources MAY disallow named logs and provide only the default, null-named log. That log has no implicit security credentials and notifications go into it with no further checking.
sections.eli5: If many people write in the same notebook, each note says who wrote it and which room it came from. You can also keep several notebooks, with different people allowed to read each one.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The module is registered as notificationLogMIB under mib-2 at number 92, and has three sections.

  • Configuration (nlmConfig) controls how much the log can hold and which notifications are logged. Its table of logs says what logs exist and how they work, and the choice of what to log depends on filters in the snmpNotifyFilterTable of the SNMP Notification MIB (RFC 2573).
  • Statistics (nlmStats) holds counters for notifications logged and discarded, so you can see the effect of capacity settings and resource problems.
  • Log (nlmLog) holds the notifications themselves.

The conformance section requires compliant systems to implement the configuration, statistics and log groups. A further date group is mandatory only on systems that keep wall clock date and time.
sections.eli5: The diary has three parts: the rules for how to write in it, a tally of how many entries were written or thrown away, and the entries themselves.

sections.title: The Log and Variable Tables
sections.content:
Each log entry is indexed by log name and by nlmLogIndex, an integer that increases as entries are made. An entry records the time (nlmLogTime, the value of sysUpTime when it was logged), the local date and time on systems that can supply it, the source engine ID, the transport address and domain it was received from, the context engine ID, the context name and the notification's object identifier.

For SNMPv1 traps the engine ID cannot be taken from the PDU, so the transport address identifies the source. The RFC warns that the address may not uniquely identify the engine, because an engine that uses DHCP or NAT may share its address with other devices.

The variables from a notification's varbind list go in a second table, indexed by log name, notification index and variable index. The value is kept as a discriminated union: nlmLogVariableValueType says which one of the value objects is filled in, with a separate object for each distinct SNMP data type. An application can therefore rebuild the information in the original notification PDU from the log.
sections.eli5: Each diary entry has a number, a time stamp and who sent it. Extra details go on a separate sheet, with a note saying what kind of detail each one is.

sections.title: Limits, Aging and Polling
sections.content:
Two global settings control how much is kept. nlmConfigGlobalEntryLimit is the maximum number of entries across all logs, where 0 means no limit. nlmConfigGlobalAgeOut is the number of minutes a notification SHOULD be kept, with a default of 1440 (24 hours) and 0 meaning no age out. Each named log also has its own nlmConfigLogEntryLimit.

If a limit is lowered while entries exist, the oldest are discarded. The global entry limit takes precedence over the age-out and per-log limits, even if the discarded entry is younger than the age-out time. When adding an entry would exceed a limit or the system resources, the oldest entry SHOULD be removed to make room. Entries removed for that reason are counted as bumped. Entries aged out are not counted that way.

A collector can poll without losing its place. The RFC suggests keeping the highest index retrieved, starting from there on the next poll, and checking sysUpTime for a discontinuity that would have reset the index and possibly lost entries. The index wraps back to 1 if it ever reaches its maximum.
sections.eli5: The notebook has a limited number of pages. When it is full, the oldest page is torn out to make room. To catch up, you remember the last page you read and carry on from there.

sections.title: Example: Logging Only Link Changes
sections.content:
The RFC shows how to set up a named log called links that records only linkUp and linkDown notifications. In the log configuration table the log gets the filter name link-status, an entry limit of 0, an admin status of enabled, non-volatile storage and an active row status.

The filter itself is built in snmpNotifyFilterTable. The object snmpTraps is 1.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.5, with linkDown as snmpTraps.3 and linkUp as snmpTraps.4. Two filter entries, one for each of those, are set to include.
sections.eli5: You tell the diary to write down only two kinds of alarm, the "link went up" and "link went down" bells, and ignore the rest.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Section 6 of the RFC only points back to the security discussion in the overview. That discussion notes that access control for the objects in a notification can only be checked where the notification is created, so it is possible only for locally generated ones, and only when credentials are available.

For a named log, the credentials of the creator stay attached to it. The system MUST use them and apply the same access control as a Notification Originator (RFC 2573) when putting local notifications in it. For remotely generated notifications the system SHOULD NOT apply access control, and security is left to the normal access control on the log.

The RFC also warns that managers setting the global entry limit or age-out to different values can disturb each other, so that some notifications are deleted before another application sees them. This could be used for a denial-of-service attack, and methods for countering it are left for further study.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can change the notebook's page limit might make pages vanish before others read them. The authors noticed this and said they had no fix yet.
